subject: ent
title: Stridor and Congenital Laryngeal Lesions

steps.tx: **Laryngomalacia** is the commonest congenital cause of stridor, where floppy supraglottic structures collapse inward on inspiration because aryepiglottic folds are short, arytenoid mucosa is redundant and the epiglottis folds into an omega shape. Noise begins in the first weeks, worsens supine or feeding and improves prone. Most infants outgrow it by eighteen months as cartilage stiffens, needing only feeding support and reflux care meanwhile.
steps.say: Floppy supraglottic collapse on inspiration gives the commonest congenital stridor in infants. Short folds with redundant mucosa and omega epiglottis produce the endoscopic picture. Most infants are free of disease by toddler age as cartilage stiffens naturally.

vis.alt: Endoscopic and coronal anatomy of laryngomalacia with omega epiglottis and prolapsing arytenoid tissue.
vis.caption: Laryngomalacia airway anatomy. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The **omega shaped epiglottis** is the visual signature at flexible endoscopy, curled laterally on itself above prolapsing arytenoid cushions that obstruct the inlet with each breath. Stridor is inspiratory, monophonic and low pitched because the lesion sits above the folds. Severe disease gives failure to thrive, apnoea and cor pulmonale, converting watchful waiting into supraglottoplasty where redundant tissue is trimmed and folds divided.
steps.say: Curled epiglottis above prolapsing cushions gives the visual signature at endoscopy. Inspiratory noise localises disease above the folds anatomically. Severe growth failure needs tissue trimming surgery.

steps.tx: **Congenital subglottic stenosis** narrows the cricoid ring, congenitally small or thickened after neonatal intubation injury, and presents with biphasic stridor and recurrent croup like episodes that respond poorly to standard therapy. Cotton Myer grading sizes the obstruction by tube fit. Mild disease observes, while severe stenosis needs expansion laryngoplasty or resection because the ring cannot stretch around scar.
steps.say: Cricoid narrowing gives biphasic stridor with recurrent croup episodes in infants. Tube fit grading sizes obstruction for treatment decisions objectively. Severe stenosis needs expansion surgery because scarred ring cannot stretch.

steps.tx: A **laryngeal web** bridges the anterior folds from incomplete recanalisation, producing weak cry, hoarseness and biphasic obstruction proportional to web thickness. Thin webs divide endoscopically, while thick webs with subglottic extension need open repair and keel placement to prevent reformation. Associated chromosome deletion syndromes are screened when webs accompany other congenital anomalies in the newborn period.
steps.say: Anterior fold bridging gives weak cry with biphasic obstruction in newborns. Thin webs divide endoscopically while thick webs need open repair. Associated anomalies need syndrome screening in newborns.

steps.tx: **Subglottic haemangioma** proliferates in early infancy below the cords, producing biphasic stridor that worsens as the lesion grows over the first months, often with cutaneous haemangiomas as a clue. Endoscopy finds a compressible reddish subglottic mass that must not be biopsied casually. Beta blocker therapy has replaced much surgery, shrinking lesions while the airway is watched in hospital during initiation.
steps.say: Subglottic vascular growth produces biphasic stridor worsening over early months. Skin haemangiomas provide a clue to airway disease presence. Medical shrinkage therapy has replaced much surgery currently.

steps.tx: **Acute epiglottitis** is bacterial cellulitis of the epiglottis in a toxic febrile child who drools, sits tripod forward and must never have the throat inspected with a depressor outside theatre. Lateral imaging gives the thumb sign of swollen epiglottis when imaging is safe to obtain. Securing the airway by intubation in theatre precedes antibiotics, and the swollen cherry red epiglottis confirms diagnosis at laryngoscopy.
steps.say: Toxic drooling children sitting forward have epiglottitis until airway is secured safely. Throat inspection outside theatre is dangerous because complete obstruction follows fatally. Theatre intubation is first before antibiotics in priority order.

vis.alt: Lateral neck image with thumbprint sign of swollen epiglottis in acute epiglottitis.
vis.caption: Thumbprint sign of epiglottitis. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The **thumb sign** on lateral neck film and the cherry red epiglottis at laryngoscopy pair as the imaging and endoscopic signatures of epiglottitis, while vaccination has shifted disease toward older children and adults. Adults present with severe sore throat out of proportion to pharyngeal findings and tolerate flexible endoscopy for diagnosis. Any age group with drooling and distress follows the same airway first rule without exception.
steps.say: Thumb shaped swelling on film pairs with cherry red epiglottis at laryngoscopy. Vaccination has shifted disease toward older children and adults recently. Drooling with distress needs airway first management always.

steps.tx: **Croup**, laryngotracheobronchitis, is viral subglottic oedema in toddlers with barking cough, inspiratory stridor and steeple sign narrowing on imaging, usually worse at night. Nebulised adrenaline and steroids relieve obstruction while hospital observation watches for rebound. The contrast with epiglottitis is bedside gold: croup children bark without drooling or toxicity, epiglottitis children drool without barking and look toxic.
steps.say: Viral subglottic swelling gives barking cough with night stridor in toddlers. Steroids with nebulised therapy relieve obstruction during observation. Drooling toxicity without bark separates epiglottitis clearly.

vis.alt: Neck radiograph with steeple sign of subglottic narrowing in croup.
vis.caption: Steeple sign of croup. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The **steeple sign** reflects subglottic oedema tapering the airway like a church steeple, while thumb sign reflects epiglottic swelling above the cords, and pairing them anchors radiology questions. **Biphasic stridor** in any child localises to glottis or subglottis, inspiratory stridor to supraglottis and expiratory wheeze to lower airway, so sound phase alone triages endoscopy urgency before instruments are touched.
steps.say: Steeple narrowing is subglottic while thumb swelling is supraglottic on films. Sound phase localises obstruction level before instruments are used. Biphasic noise indicates glottic or subglottic disease.

steps.tx: **Laryngotracheobronchitis** severe enough to need intubation uses a smaller tube for the swollen subglottis and plans extubation only after an air leak returns around the tube. Repeated croup episodes in one child reopen the congenital stenosis differential rather than repeating viral labels. Growth, feeding and voice review continue after every severe episode because subglottic injury declares itself slowly over subsequent months.
steps.say: Intubation for severe croup needs smaller tubes for swollen subglottis. Air leak return guides safe extubation timing afterwards. Repeated episodes need stenosis exclusion rather than viral labels.

cards.b: Omega epiglottis with prolapsing arytenoids, inspiratory stridor, improves prone, outgrown by 18 months; supraglottoplasty if severe.
Thumb: swollen epiglottis in epiglottitis. Steeple: subglottic narrowing in croup.
Never inspect with depressor outside theatre; secure airway by theatre intubation before antibiotics.

keys: Sound phase localises the obstruction level
Recurrent croup means exclude subglottic stenosis
Drooling without bark is epiglottitis, bark without drool is croup
